purpose: Exercise restic 0.19.1 locally against ACL/xattrs, sparse files, hardlinks, symlinks and unusual names, backing up and restoring both to a local (ext4) repo and to a repo on /mnt/c (drvfs, C:\Users\example\gap-resolution-restic), then diff metadata after each restore to directly narrow open_gaps[3].
preregistered: If the local (ext4-to-ext4) round trip preserves every captured metadata field (mode, POSIX ACL, user xattr, sha256, symlink target, hardlink grouping) exactly, and the drvfs (/mnt/c) round trip preserves file content (sha256), symlink targets and hardlink grouping but drops POSIX mode/ACL/user-xattr (the expected 9p/drvfs limitation, since drvfs synthesizes a fixed permission view and does not support Linux xattrs), this settles open_gaps[3] for the filesystem-semantics subset as: restic round-trips filesystem semantics correctly end-to-end on a POSIX target, and preserves data integrity but not POSIX permission metadata on a drvfs/NTFS-backed target -- narrowing the gap from 'untested' to 'measured, with permission loss on Windows-backed targets recorded as a known limitation' rather than eliminating it (long-term retention and true NTFS-native ACL mapping remain out of scope for a same-day check). Any restic init/backup/restore/check exit code != 0, or a sha256 mismatch on the same-filesystem round trip, would refute the assumption that restic correctly round-trips this fixture and must be recorded as a failure, not smoothed over.

result: Local (ext4-to-ext4) restic backup/restore round trip preserved every captured metadata field exactly (mode, POSIX ACL text, user xattr name+value, sha256 content, symlink target, hardlink grouping) -- diff-local.json shows zero changed/added/missing paths. The drvfs (/mnt/c) round trip preserved content (sha256 identical for every file including the 10MiB sparse file), symlink target, and hardlink grouping (hardlink-src.txt and hardlink-dst.txt still share one inode_group after restore), but every restored entry's POSIX mode collapsed to 0777 and its getfacl output collapsed to a generic 'user::rwx/group::rwx/other::rwx', and both the POSIX ACL xattr (system.posix_acl_access) and the user xattr (user.gap_check) were absent on the drvfs-restored files. All restic init/backup/restore/check invocations exited 0 with no reported errors on both targets.

verdict_impact.explanation: Confirms restic 0.19.1 is safe and correct for the filesystem-semantics subset of open_gaps[3] when both source and destination are POSIX filesystems (ACLs, xattrs, sparse content, hardlinks, symlinks, unusual names all round-trip byte-for-byte), which supports restic's incumbent winner status. It also produces a concrete, previously-missing measurement for the drvfs/NTFS-backed-target sub-claim: content integrity and link structure survive, but POSIX permission/xattr metadata does not -- this is a real, now-documented limitation rather than an assumption, so it narrows but does not close open_gaps[3] (long-term retention and genuine NTFS ACL mapping remain untested).

limitations: Single run, no retry/fishing per the preregistration rule; both round trips happened to succeed cleanly, so there is no adverse-outcome sample to compare against.

The drvfs mode/ACL loss is attributable to the 9p/drvfs mount driver's fixed permission view, not necessarily representative of native NTFS-on-Windows or a true CIFS/SMB target; this environment has no bare-metal NTFS or SMB mount to test.
Long-term retention policy (weeks/months) is explicitly out of scope on a same-day timescale, per gap-triage.json's own blocker text for open_gaps[3].

Sparse-file disk-block preservation (vs. logical size) was not part of the preregistered metadata manifest and was only spot-checked with `du`, which showed the local restore fully materializing the 10MiB file (apparent size == actual blocks); this is a restic restore-sparsity behavior note, not a settled claim, and is not counted toward settles_gap.
Repository password used was a fixed test string ('gap-resolution-20260922-test'), acceptable for a disposable scratch repo but not representative of a production secret-handling path.

/mnt/c/Users/example/gap-resolution-restic and .../gap-resolution-restic-restore are left on disk under the Windows host's Public folder as durable evidence; they were not deleted after the check (no cleanup requested by this check's scope, unlike the app-state check which requires process cleanup).

Absolute paths recorded above have the host username and the Windows target user-folder segment normalized to this repo's publication-hygiene placeholder (scripts/validate.py PRIVATE_CONTENT rules); only the identifying name segment is normalized, the rest of each path structure is unchanged from what was actually used.
